case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a district court deciding a compassionate-release motion under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A) may treat as part of its “extraordinary and compelling reasons” a set of considerations that could also be framed as grounds to vacate the conviction or sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A) (compassionate release; “extraordinary and compelling reasons”), in interaction with 28 U.S.C. § 2255 (post-conviction vacatur remedy) and the Sentencing Commission policy statement U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Fernandez argues that § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s text and the First Step Act’s design give district courts broad discretion to consider the “totality of the circumstances” when deciding whether “extraordinary and compelling reasons” warrant a discretionary sentence reduction. On that view, the mere fact that some of the same underlying facts or arguments might also be characterized as § 2255-type claims should not categorically bar a court from considering them in the compassionate-release calculus—especially when combined with other individualized factors (e.g., unusual sentencing consequences, fairness concerns, rehabilitation, health/age, or other post-sentencing developments). Petitioner emphasizes that § 3582 relief is not vacatur and does not ‘re-litigate’ guilt; it is a limited, discretionary sentence-modification mechanism constrained by statutory factors (including § 3553(a)) and guided by the Commission’s policy statements, which together prevent § 3582 from becoming an end-run around habeas rules.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that challenges going to the validity of the conviction or sentence—i.e., the ‘proper office’ of § 2255—are categorically excluded from § 3582(c)(1)(A). In the government’s view, allowing courts to treat § 2255-type arguments as “extraordinary and compelling reasons” would undermine Congress’s carefully reticulated post-conviction framework (timeliness limits, procedural default, and strict limits on second-or-successive petitions), invite relitigation of convictions/sentences through a discretionary resentencing portal, and force district courts (and previously the BOP gatekeeper) to adjudicate issues like innocence or legal error outside § 2255’s rules. The government therefore seeks a bright-line rule: compassionate release can account for post-sentencing circumstances (medical, family, age, etc.) but cannot incorporate attacks on legal validity that belong in § 2255.
key_precedents: Concepcion v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2389 (2022)
United States v. Trenkler (1st Cir.) (referenced in argument as post-First Step Act compassionate release authority)
United States v. Piggott, 2022 WL 118632 (S.D.N.Y. Jan. 12, 2022)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s Concepcion-based point is the strongest for petitioner, but Concepcion speaks to what information a court may consider once Congress has authorized resentencing; it does not expand § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s antecedent gateway of what qualifies as an “extraordinary and compelling” reason. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right that the remedy is only a reduction, not vacatur, but Justice Barrett’s structural channeling point persuades me that allowing § 2255-type legal-invalidity/innocence claims to supply the threshold predicate would still function as an end-run around Congress’s reticulated limits on collateral review, because courts would necessarily adjudicate the very validity questions § 2255 assigns elsewhere to decide whether the asserted “extraordinary” circumstance exists. Dillon’s description of § 3582 as “circumscribed” reinforces a narrow, finality-preserving reading: courts may consider intervening factual circumstances (and lawful sentencing developments) in exercising discretion once a proper compassionate-release predicate is shown, but alleged invalidity cannot itself be that predicate. This minimalist reconciliation respects both statutes’ work without imposing an evidentiary “gag rule” broader than necessary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—grounded in Concepcion—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express prohibition on considering legal developments cannot carry the day because Concepcion presupposes Congress has already opened a resentencing lane and speaks to what may be considered within that lane, not what qualifies as the threshold “extraordinary and compelling” predicate. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, reading that predicate to include claims whose gravamen is legal invalidity would, as a matter of statutory structure and original public meaning, let § 3582 swallow § 2255’s exclusive and reticulated limits on timeliness and successive motions, effectively converting a narrow exception to finality (“may not modify” with enumerated exceptions) into a collateral-review substitute. Justice Sotomayor’s remedy-based distinction (reduction vs. vacatur) does not cure the problem, because district courts would still have to decide the same validity questions Congress assigned to § 2255 to determine whether the asserted “extraordinary” circumstance exists. Dillon’s description of § 3582 as “circumscribed” thus properly informs the textual reconciliation: the sentence-modification inquiry assumes a legally valid judgment and permits discretion only once a proper compassionate-release-type predicate is shown.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express categorical bar and, under Concepcion, courts generally may consider intervening information once Congress opens a resentencing channel. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Concepcion presupposes threshold authority; it does not expand what qualifies as an “extraordinary and compelling” predicate, and Dillon’s description of § 3582 as “circumscribed” confirms it is a narrow exception to finality that assumes the judgment’s legal validity. Allowing legal-invalidity/innocence theories to supply the gateway would, in substance, reroute § 2255 claims around Congress’s reticulated limits (timeliness, successive motions, default), because the court would still have to adjudicate those legal questions to decide whether the asserted “extraordinary” circumstance exists. Justice Sotomayor’s remedy-based limit (reduction only, no vacatur) does not cure that structural conflict: the evasion occurs at the threshold inquiry, not at the label of the relief.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett press the strongest point: allowing legal-invalidity arguments to supply the “extraordinary and compelling” gateway could erode § 2255’s timeliness and successive-motion limits by creating a functional end-run. But that structural concern does not justify an atextual categorical carveout from § 3582(c)(1)(A), because the statute authorizes only a discretionary sentence reduction (not vacatur) and already cabins relief through exhaustion, § 3553(a), and the district court’s ability to reject attempts to reli­tigate barred merits questions. Concepcion, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, sets the baseline that once Congress opens a sentence-modification mechanism, courts may consider relevant intervening developments absent a clear statutory prohibition—and nothing in § 3582(c)(1)(A) expressly requires courts to be blind to legal changes when assessing whether continued incarceration is extraordinary in real-world terms. Dillon’s “circumscribed” language, cited by Justice Barrett, supports limiting the remedy and procedure, but it does not compel importing § 2255’s subject-matter exclusivity into § 3582’s gateway where Congress did not write that limitation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s (and Justice Barrett’s) strongest point is structural: if alleged legal invalidity can itself satisfy the “extraordinary and compelling” gateway, § 3582(c)(1)(A) risks becoming a de facto substitute for § 2255 and eroding Congress’s limits on successive and untimely collateral attacks. But that concern does not justify an atextual categorical carveout from the statutory phrase “extraordinary and compelling reasons”; as Justice Sotomayor notes, § 3582 offers only a discretionary reduction (not vacatur), and Dillon’s “circumscribed” language is better read as a constraint on remedy and posture rather than a subject-matter exclusion. Concepcion, while not expanding the gateway, reinforces that once Congress opens a sentence-modification mechanism, courts may consider relevant intervening information absent a clear prohibition—and nothing in § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s text clearly bars legal developments from informing whether continued incarceration is extraordinary, so long as courts do not adjudicate (or effectively relitigate) a barred § 2255 claim. I therefore would hold that validity-type assertions cannot be used to obtain vacatur or a merits determination of innocence/invalidity in this posture, but may be considered as part of the holistic “extraordinary and compelling” and § 3553(a) assessment without rewriting the threshold.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s Concepcion point presses hardest because § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express subject-matter bar, but Concepcion presupposes Congress has already conferred resentencing authority and does not redefine the statute’s threshold “extraordinary and compelling” gateway. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively explain that treating alleged legal invalidity or innocence as that gateway would, in substance, recreate § 2255 review while discarding Congress’s reticulated limits on timeliness and successive motions—an end-run inconsistent with separation-of-powers principles and Dillon’s description of § 3582 as a “circumscribed” exception to finality. Justice Sotomayor’s “no vacatur” limit does not cure the problem, because a court would still have to adjudicate the very § 2255-type merits question to decide whether the asserted “extraordinary” circumstance exists. I therefore would allow intervening facts and lawful sentencing developments to inform discretion and § 3553(a) once a proper compassionate-release basis is shown, but not permit validity challenges to supply the predicate basis for § 3582 relief.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s Concepcion-based point is the best for petitioner, but Concepcion presupposes Congress has already opened a resentencing lane and speaks to what information may be considered within that lane—not to redefining § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s threshold gateway. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly emphasize the structural clash: if alleged legal invalidity or innocence can itself be the “extraordinary and compelling” predicate, § 2255’s timeliness and successive-motion limits are effectively bypassed, because courts must adjudicate the very merits questions Congress channeled elsewhere to decide whether the predicate exists. Dillon’s description of § 3582 as “circumscribed” reinforces that this narrow exception to finality assumes the judgment’s legal validity in this posture, even if background facts may later inform § 3553(a) once a proper compassionate-release predicate is shown. Petitioner’s proposed “no vacatur” limiting principle (Justice Sotomayor) does not cure the end-run problem, because the substance of the inquiry—not the formal label of the remedy—would still convert § 3582 into a collateral-review surrogate.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s Concepcion-based point—that absent an express prohibition courts may consider a wide range of information—does not answer the antecedent textual and structural question: what kinds of reasons may satisfy § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s “extraordinary and compelling” gateway in the first place. Concepcion presupposes Congress has opened a resentencing channel and then addresses the scope of inputs within that channel; here, reading the gateway to include claims whose gravamen is legal invalidity would, as the Chief Justice argues, functionally displace Congress’s reticulated § 2255 scheme (including timeliness and successive-motion limits) by relabeling collateral attacks as compassionate release. Justice Sotomayor’s remedy-focused limit (no vacatur) is insufficient under Dillon’s description of § 3582 as “circumscribed,” because the substance of the inquiry would still require adjudicating validity to decide whether the asserted “extraordinary” circumstance exists. I would hold courts may consider post-sentencing factual developments and lawful sentencing factors under § 3553(a) once a proper compassionate-release predicate exists, but alleged invalidity or innocence cannot itself be that predicate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s channeling/finality concern is the hardest point: if “extraordinary and compelling” became a substitute for § 2255, Congress’s reticulated limits would be undermined. But I do not think we avoid that only by a categorical subject-matter carveout; rather, we can respect § 2255 by policing the nature of the § 3582 proceeding—no adjudication that the conviction or sentence is unlawful, no vacatur, and no relitigation of claims that § 2255 would bar—while still allowing courts to consider intervening developments for their practical consequences in deciding whether continued incarceration is extraordinary and compelling. Justice Barrett’s worry that courts must necessarily decide the underlying legal question to assess extraordinariness overstates the problem, because district courts routinely assess uncertainty and equity without issuing a merits ruling, and Concepcion (as Justice Kagan stresses) sets the baseline against atextual exclusions once Congress has authorized a sentence-reduction mechanism. Dillon’s “circumscribed” language, in my view, limits the remedy and posture (discretionary reduction within statutory constraints) rather than imposing a categorical evidentiary blindfold that Congress did not write into § 3582(c)(1)(A).

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) creates a narrow exception to the general rule of finality in § 3582(c), authorizing only a limited sentence-modification based on “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” not a collateral attack on the conviction or sentence’s legal validity. Dillon v. United States characterizes § 3582(c) proceedings as circumscribed modifications rather than plenary resentencings, and allowing § 2255-type validity challenges to supply the “extraordinary and compelling” predicate would effectively bypass Congress’s carefully reticulated § 2255 framework (including limits on successive petitions and procedural rules). A categorical exclusion limited to claims that fall within the “proper office” of § 2255 preserves institutional legitimacy and respects Congress’s allocation of post-conviction remedies while leaving district courts ample room to consider truly post-sentencing circumstances and then apply § 3553(a). Any broader reading risks turning compassionate release into an end run around habeas, an expansion better left to Congress or the Sentencing Commission’s policy statements (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13) rather than judicial innovation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of § 3582(c)(1)(A) create a narrow exception to the general rule that a court “may not modify a term of imprisonment once it has been imposed,” permitting reduction only for “extraordinary and compelling reasons” consistent with Sentencing Commission policy statements—not as an alternative vehicle to contest the conviction’s or sentence’s legal validity. Congress separately provided the exclusive post-conviction mechanism for such validity challenges in § 2255, complete with strict limits on timeliness and second-or-successive motions; reading § 3582 to encompass § 2255-type claims would defeat that careful design and expand the exception beyond what the words reasonably bear. Nothing in the original public meaning of “compassionate release” or “extraordinary and compelling reasons” as enacted in the Sentencing Reform Act suggests it included legal-error or innocence claims traditionally addressed by habeas/§ 2255, and this Court has treated such claims with skepticism absent constitutional error. Concepcion v. United States does not alter that conclusion because it concerns what courts may consider within an authorized resentencing proceeding, not whether § 3582 authorizes a collateral attack that § 2255 assigns elsewhere.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a limited sentence-modification inquiry keyed to whether "extraordinary and compelling reasons" warrant a reduction and whether the reduction is consistent with applicable Sentencing Commission policy statements, not a collateral attack on the conviction or sentence. Reading that phrase to include claims that the conviction or sentence is legally invalid would effectively circumvent Congress’s carefully reticulated post-conviction scheme in 28 U.S.C. § 2255, including strict limits on timeliness, procedural default, and second-or-successive petitions. Concepcion recognizes broad discretion within authorized sentence-modification proceedings, but it does not license courts to repurpose § 3582 into an alternate vehicle for § 2255-type challenges, particularly where Congress has provided a specific and exclusive remedial framework for such claims. Practical consequences also counsel against the petitioner’s approach, which would predictably invite routine relitigation of validity issues through a discretionary “compassionate release” portal and burden district courts while undermining finality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a discretionary sentence reduction when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” warrant it, and nothing in its text creates a categorical bar merely because some of the same facts could be characterized as a § 2255-type claim; the court still must apply § 3553(a) and any applicable Sentencing Commission guidance, which prevents § 3582 from becoming de facto vacatur. Concepcion v. United States confirms that, absent an express prohibition, district courts in First Step Act sentence-modification proceedings may consider a wide range of intervening facts and legal developments, supporting a totality-of-the-circumstances approach to what is “extraordinary and compelling.” The government’s bright-line exclusion risks denying relief in the rare but real cases where continued incarceration is unjust in light of post-sentencing developments and would disproportionately harm vulnerable defendants, while the existing procedural safeguards (exhaustion, § 3553(a), and the limited remedy of sentence reduction rather than invalidation) mitigate end-run concerns. Herrera v. Collins underscores that innocence-based and legality-based challenges have a distinct remedial home, but it does not require courts to ignore overlapping considerations when exercising Congress’s separate, equitable compassionate-release authority under § 3582.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a discretionary sentence “reduc[tion]” when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” warrant it, subject to § 3553(a), the rehabilitation-alone bar in 28 U.S.C. § 994(t), and consistency with applicable Commission policy statements—none of which textually imposes the government’s categorical exclusion for considerations that could also be framed under § 2255. Concepcion v. United States teaches that in congressionally authorized sentence-modification proceedings, district courts may consider intervening changes of law or fact and should not be saddled with extra-textual limits absent clear statutory direction; that principle fits the First Step Act’s shift away from BOP gatekeeping toward judicial discretion. The proper reconciliation is functional, not formal: a court may not use § 3582 to vacate a conviction or adjudicate a collateral attack, but it may consider overlapping facts or legal developments as part of a holistic “extraordinary and compelling” assessment so long as the remedy remains a sentence reduction and the court adheres to § 3553(a) and any applicable § 1B1.13 constraints. Reading § 3582 to forbid any overlap with § 2255 would create an atextual bright line that undermines workability and the statute’s broad, purposefully open-ended “extraordinary and compelling” language.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes only a limited “sentence reduction” based on “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” not a vehicle to revisit the legal validity of a conviction or sentence—work Congress assigned to § 2255 with its specific limits on timeliness, procedural default, and successive petitions. Reading § 3582 to encompass § 2255-type claims would evade that carefully reticulated framework and blur separation-of-powers boundaries by effectively creating an alternative postconviction remedy Congress did not enact. Dillon v. United States confirms that § 3582 sentence-modification proceedings are narrow in scope and do not permit plenary resentencing or correction of underlying errors outside the statute’s authorization. Whatever discretion Concepcion recognizes in certain resentencing contexts, it does not supply authority to convert compassionate release into a collateral-attack surrogate contrary to the text and structure of §§ 3582 and 2255.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) is a narrow sentence-modification provision triggered by “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” whereas Congress separately established § 2255 as the exclusive post-conviction mechanism to challenge the validity of a conviction or sentence, complete with strict timeliness and second-or-successive limits. Allowing § 2255-type attacks to be recast as “extraordinary and compelling” would functionally circumvent that carefully reticulated framework and invite relitigation outside the procedural rules Congress imposed in § 2255. Concepcion confirms that district-court discretion in sentence-modification proceedings exists only within the resentencing mechanism Congress created, and it does not authorize importing a different remedial scheme (vacatur) into § 3582. History and finality concerns reflected in cases like Herrera v. Collins reinforce that claims of legal invalidity and innocence are addressed through collateral review channels, not ad hoc discretionary reductions under § 3582.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a court to “reduce the term of imprisonment” based on “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” but it does not confer power to adjudicate the legal validity of a conviction or sentence; Congress provided that distinct function through § 2255, with specific procedural and successive-petition limits that would be undermined if the same arguments could be repackaged as compassionate-release reasons. Concepcion v. United States confirms broad discretion in sentence-modification proceedings only within the bounds “set forth by Congress in a statute,” and the structure here—pairing § 3582’s limited modification mechanism with § 2255’s exclusive vacatur remedy—signals that validity attacks are out of place in § 3582’s threshold inquiry. A district court may consider post-sentencing developments and individualized circumstances under § 3553(a), but it must take the conviction and sentence as legally valid unless and until vacated through § 2255 (or direct review). This reading preserves methodological consistency with the text and Congress’s reticulated post-conviction framework while leaving room for compassionate release to operate in its traditional domain (medical, family, age, and comparable circumstances), consistent with applicable policy statements such as U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a discretionary sentence reduction when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” warrant it and the § 3553(a) factors support it, and nothing in that text imposes a categorical bar on considering facts merely because they could also be packaged as § 2255 arguments. Concepcion v. United States confirms the “largely unlimited” tradition of sentencing courts considering all relevant information in sentence-modification proceedings unless Congress clearly restricts that discretion, and here Congress did not write an explicit § 2255-type exclusion into § 3582. Properly understood, allowing such considerations as part of the totality does not convert compassionate release into vacatur—finality and channeling concerns are protected because § 3582 cannot set aside the conviction, remains bounded by § 3553(a), and must be exercised with procedural fairness (including avoiding relitigation where law-of-the-case or prior adjudications resolve the issue). A bright-line rule forbidding any overlap would be overinclusive and risk unjust results in atypical cases where practical consequences and equity strongly support a modest sentence reduction without reopening the judgment.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether courts deciding compassionate-release motions under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A) may treat as part of the “extraordinary and compelling reasons” analysis circumstances that could also be framed as collateral attacks on the conviction or sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A) (compassionate release / sentence modification for “extraordinary and compelling reasons”), in interaction with 28 U.S.C. § 2255 (post-conviction vacatur remedy), and the Sentencing Commission policy statement U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13 (as referenced in the record).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Fernandez argues that § 3582(c)(1)(A) confers broad, discretionary authority to reduce a lawfully imposed sentence when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” exist, and nothing in the statute categorically forbids courts from considering as part of the totality-of-circumstances analysis facts or legal developments that might also be styled as § 2255 grounds. He contends that § 3582 is not a substitute for vacatur—courts still must apply § 3553(a) and decide whether and how much to reduce the sentence—so allowing overlap does not collapse the § 2255 regime. He further relies on the First Step Act’s design (removing the BOP gatekeeping role and expanding access to judicial consideration) and on Supreme Court language describing sentencing-modification discretion as broad, arguing that district courts can manage any floodgates through ordinary tools (law-of-the-case, waiver/forfeiture principles, and the demanding ‘extraordinary and compelling’ threshold).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is a limited sentence-modification mechanism and not a vehicle to relitigate the legality/validity of a conviction or sentence, which Congress instead channeled into § 2255 with strict procedural limits (timeliness, successive-petition bars, and substantive standards). On the government’s view, allowing courts to treat § 2255-type claims (e.g., innocence or sentencing error) as ‘extraordinary and compelling’ would create an end-run around § 2255’s constraints and effectively authorize collateral review without Congress’s safeguards. The government thus seeks a categorical or near-categorical rule excluding ‘attacks on the validity’ of the conviction or sentence from the § 3582 extraordinary-and-compelling inquiry, even when packaged as one factor among several, to preserve the separation between discretionary leniency (3582) and legal invalidity (2255).
key_precedents: Concepcion v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2389 (2022)
United States v. Trenkler (1st Cir.) (as discussed in argument/briefing context)
United States v. Piggott, 2022 WL 118632 (S.D.N.Y. Jan. 12, 2022) (district court authority/totality analysis, cited in the appendix excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest textual point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) lacks an express categorical bar and Concepcion speaks broadly—has real force, but it does not overcome the structural boundary Congress created by channeling legality challenges into § 2255 with distinct gatekeeping. As Justice Kagan persuasively frames it, Concepcion’s “any arguments” discretion operates only within the “specific statutory authorization,” and § 3582 authorizes a discretionary reduction premised on a valid judgment, not adjudication of unlawfulness; Dillon’s description of § 3582 as a limited modification proceeding reinforces that divide. A narrow, administrable holding excluding arguments that in substance attack the conviction or sentence’s legal validity—while allowing courts to consider post-sentencing facts and nonretroactive legal changes as equitable context—best preserves finality and institutional legitimacy without reading extra limits into the statute. Petitioners remain able to seek vacatur through § 2255; § 3582 should not become collateral review by another name.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express categorical bar and Concepcion allows consideration of “any arguments”—cannot overcome the statute’s text and structure, which begin from a rule of finality (“may not modify”) and then create narrow, enumerated exceptions. As Justice Gorsuch notes (relying on Dillon), § 3582 is a limited sentence-modification mechanism that presupposes a valid judgment; it is not a plenary resentencing or a collateral-review substitute, so “extraordinary and compelling reasons” cannot be read to include claims that the conviction or sentence is unlawful. Concepcion’s breadth operates only within “specific statutory authorization,” and it does not supply authority to do the work Congress assigned to § 2255, with its reticulated timeliness and successive-motion limits—limits that would be functionally nullified if defendants could relabel validity challenges as compassionate-release factors. Justice Kagan’s administrable line reinforces the same textualist point: courts may consider post-sentencing facts and equitable context, but must exclude arguments whose substance is legal invalidity reserved to § 2255.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the textual-silence point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) nowhere expressly forbids considering circumstances that resemble § 2255 claims, and Concepcion’s language about considering “any arguments” is broad. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, Concepcion’s breadth operates only within the “specific statutory authorization,” and § 3582’s authorization is a narrow exception to finality that presupposes a valid judgment, while Congress separately created § 2255 as the reticulated vehicle for illegality challenges with strict gatekeeping; reading “extraordinary and compelling” to include validity attacks would create an end-run that nullifies that scheme. Dillon’s characterization of § 3582 as a limited sentence-modification proceeding reinforces that structural boundary: compassionate release can weigh post-sentencing facts and equitable considerations, but it cannot be converted into collateral review in substance. The practical consequences—relitigation and erosion of finality—confirm that the better textualist reading is to exclude § 2255-type invalidity claims from qualifying as “extraordinary and compelling reasons.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—the need to prevent an “end-run” around § 2255—has real force, but it cannot justify a categorical atextual carveout from § 3582(c)(1)(A), which nowhere instructs courts to disregard circumstances merely because they resemble a legality argument. Dillon (as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes) confirms § 3582 is a limited, discretionary sentence-modification proceeding, yet that very limitation undercuts the bypass concern because the court cannot vacate a conviction or declare a sentence unlawful; it can only reduce a sentence after finding “extraordinary and compelling reasons” and reassessing § 3553(a). Concepcion’s insistence that courts may consider intervening developments absent express statutory limits fits here: the authorization is to “reduce” a sentence, and considering overlapping legal/factual developments as part of an equitable, individualized assessment does not transform the proceeding into collateral review. As a pragmatic matter, the demanding threshold and § 3553(a) provide administrable safeguards for finality while preserving Congress’s First Step Act choice to expand access to compassionate release for extraordinary cases, including those involving profound unfairness to vulnerable defendants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express categorical bar and that, under Concepcion, courts may consider intervening developments in authorized modification proceedings; I agree with that much. But Concepcion’s breadth is explicitly tethered to the “specific statutory authorization,” and as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize (citing Dillon), § 3582 is a limited sentence-modification mechanism that presupposes a valid judgment and authorizes only a discretionary “reduc[tion],” not adjudication of legal invalidity. Justice Jackson’s response—that the remedy is not vacatur and discretion plus § 3553(a) can police finality—doesn’t fully answer the structural problem: letting legal-invalidity claims qualify as “extraordinary and compelling” would effectively nullify § 2255’s reticulated gatekeeping by permitting the same substance to be relabeled and relitigated. A workable middle ground remains: consider new facts and even nonretroactive legal changes as equitable context, but exclude claims whose gravamen is that the conviction or sentence is unlawful.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express bar and Concepcion speaks broadly of considering intervening developments—cannot carry the weight she places on statutory silence. As Justice Kagan and the Chief observe, Concepcion’s breadth operates only within the “specific statutory authorization,” and § 3582(c) is a narrow exception to a categorical finality rule (“may not modify”), authorizing discretionary leniency on a valid judgment rather than adjudication of legal invalidity Congress separately channeled to § 2255 with gatekeeping. Dillon reinforces that boundary by describing § 3582 as a limited, non-plenary modification proceeding, which makes it textually and structurally implausible to treat “extraordinary and compelling reasons” as a backdoor for § 2255-type claims. I therefore maintain that courts may consider post-sentencing facts and even nonretroactive legal changes as equitable context, but not arguments whose substance is that the conviction or sentence was unlawful.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s textual point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) lacks an express categorical bar and that Concepcion speaks broadly about what courts may consider—has real force, but it does not answer the threshold structural question of what the proceeding is for. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Concepcion’s “any arguments” language operates only within “specific statutory authorization,” and § 3582 is a narrow exception to finality that presupposes a valid judgment; Dillon’s description of § 3582 as a limited modification proceeding reinforces that it is not collateral review in disguise. Allowing claims whose substance is legal invalidity to qualify as “extraordinary and compelling” would, in practical effect, nullify Congress’s reticulated § 2255 gatekeeping (timeliness and successive limits) and undermine finality and administrability. District courts still have broad discretion to consider post-sentencing developments and even nonretroactive legal changes as equitable context, but challenges to the conviction’s or sentence’s lawfulness belong in § 2255.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s textual point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express bar on considering circumstances that overlap with § 2255—has force, and Concepcion’s language about considering “any arguments” underscores broad discretion once a modification proceeding is properly authorized. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 3582 begins from a rule of finality (“may not modify”) and creates a narrow exception to reduce a concededly valid sentence; reading “extraordinary and compelling” to encompass claims whose substance is legal invalidity would let litigants bypass Congress’s specific, reticulated gatekeeping in § 2255. Dillon’s description of § 3582 proceedings as limited modifications, not plenary resentencings, confirms that Concepcion’s discretion operates within the authorized lane and cannot transform compassionate release into collateral review by another name. I therefore remain persuaded that courts may consider post-sentencing facts and even nonretroactive legal changes as equitable context, but should exclude arguments that in substance attack the judgment’s legality.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “end-run around § 2255” concern is the most serious structural objection, but it does not justify grafting onto § 3582(c)(1)(A) a categorical validity/invalidity bar that Congress did not write—especially given the limited remedy (a discretionary reduction, not vacatur) and the built-in constraints of the “extraordinary and compelling” threshold plus § 3553(a). Justice Kagan’s administrable line, grounded in Dillon’s description of § 3582 as “limited,” usefully clarifies that compassionate release is not a plenary resentencing, yet Dillon does not supply a text-based rule forbidding courts from considering overlapping legal developments as part of an individualized assessment; Concepcion’s emphasis on broad consideration absent express limits points the other way. On pragmatic, fairness-oriented grounds, courts can police finality by denying relief when a motion is merely relitigation, without disabling judges from addressing exceptional cases where continued imprisonment has become unusually unjust in light of intervening circumstances. Because the respondent side’s reading relies heavily on implied structural exclusivity rather than statutory text, it does not undermine my view that Congress entrusted district courts with flexible, case-specific discretion here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a limited sentence modification for “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” while Congress expressly channeled challenges to the validity of a conviction or sentence into § 2255 with strict gatekeeping rules (including timeliness and successive-petition limits); reading § 3582 to encompass § 2255-type collateral attacks would risk an end-run around that scheme and undermine the finality and orderly administration Congress chose. Concepcion v. United States confirms broad discretion within authorized sentence-modification proceedings, but it does not suggest courts may use § 3582 to perform collateral review that Congress assigned elsewhere. A narrow, administrable rule excluding arguments that function as attacks on the conviction or sentence preserves institutional legitimacy and respects the distinct roles of § 3582 and § 2255, leaving defendants to pursue validity challenges through the established post-conviction process. That approach also avoids inviting relitigation of jury verdicts and sentencing legality in a proceeding designed for discretionary leniency, consistent with the skepticism reflected in Herrera v. Collins about freestanding innocence claims absent a recognized vehicle.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) is a narrow exception to the finality of criminal judgments, authorizing only a sentence reduction when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” exist; its text does not authorize courts to adjudicate the legal validity of the conviction or sentence, a function Congress specifically assigned to § 2255 with detailed limits on timing and successive applications. Reading § 3582 to encompass § 2255-type claims would let a general sentencing-modification provision circumvent a more specific, carefully reticulated postconviction scheme, contrary to ordinary interpretive principles and Congress’s channeling of collateral review into § 2255(b), (f), and (h). This Court has policed similar end-runs in the habeas context by requiring prisoners to use the exclusive postconviction route Congress provided rather than repackaging validity challenges under other remedial vehicles. Concepcion’s recognition of broad resentencing discretion does not supply authority where Congress has not granted it, because § 3582 remains a limited modification statute, not a substitute collateral-review mechanism.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a limited sentence-modification for “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and that remedial discretion presupposes the continuing validity of the underlying conviction and sentence rather than reopening their legality. Congress specifically channeled attacks on the validity of a conviction or sentence into § 2255, with strict limits on timeliness and successive petitions, and reading § 3582 to incorporate § 2255-type claims would create an end-run around those constraints and undermine finality. Concepcion’s broad language about considering “any arguments” in sentence-modification proceedings arose in a different statutory context and cannot be used to collapse the separation Congress created between discretionary leniency (§ 3582) and collateral review (§ 2255). Consistent with Herrera’s skepticism toward freestanding innocence claims and the practical consequences for law enforcement and finality, courts should categorically exclude collateral-attack contentions from the “extraordinary and compelling reasons” inquiry.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a discretionary sentence reduction when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” warrant it and after consideration of the § 3553(a) factors; nothing in the text imposes a categorical bar on considering circumstances merely because they could also be characterized as § 2255-type arguments. Concepcion v. United States confirms that, absent an express limitation, district courts have broad latitude in sentence-modification proceedings to consider intervening legal and factual developments and to “sentence the whole person,” and that principle fits the First Step Act’s expansion of judicial access to compassionate release. The government’s proposed near-absolute exclusion would improperly “draw meaning from silence” and would unduly restrict a remedial statute designed to account for real-world inequities, while courts can still prevent end-runs around § 2255 by denying relief under the demanding “extraordinary and compelling” threshold and by applying § 3553(a) to ensure public safety and respect for finality. Allowing overlap does not convert § 3582 into vacatur: the remedy remains a discretionary sentence reduction, not invalidation of the conviction or sentence under § 2255’s framework.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a discretionary “reduc[tion]” of a concededly lawful sentence for “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” but it does not textually invite courts to adjudicate the validity of the conviction or sentence—work Congress specifically assigned to § 2255 with its distinct standards and procedural limits. Reading § 3582 to encompass § 2255-type invalidity claims would undermine statutory coherence by allowing an end-run around § 2255’s timeliness and successive-petition restrictions, even if framed as one factor among others. Concepcion confirms broad consideration of intervening law and facts in authorized sentence-modification proceedings, but it also ties that discretion to the “specific statutory authorization” and does not suggest § 3582 can be used to replicate collateral review. A workable middle ground is a categorical exclusion for claims that, in substance, attack the conviction/sentence’s legal validity, while permitting consideration of non-validity developments (e.g., health, family circumstances, rehabilitation, nonretroactive sentencing changes) within § 3582 and consistent with the Sentencing Commission’s policy statements (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) is an exception to the general rule of finality—courts “may not modify a term of imprisonment once it has been imposed”—and so must be read narrowly as authorizing discretionary leniency, not a backdoor adjudication of legal invalidity. Dillon v. United States confirms § 3582 proceedings are not plenary resentencings but limited sentence-modification mechanisms, which structurally counsels against importing into the “extraordinary and compelling reasons” inquiry claims whose proper office is collateral relief under § 2255. Allowing § 2255-type challenges to be repackaged as “extraordinary and compelling” would evade Congress’s carefully reticulated § 2255 limits (timeliness, successive-petition bars) and blur the separation between sentence modification and vacatur. Courts may consider post-sentencing facts and individualized circumstances, but they must take the conviction and sentence as given and cannot treat alleged legal errors or innocence arguments as part of the § 3582(c)(1)(A) threshold inquiry.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) is a narrow sentence-modification provision that presupposes the continuing validity of the conviction and sentence, whereas Congress specifically channeled challenges to the legality of a conviction or sentence into § 2255 with strict limits on timeliness and successive petitions. Allowing § 2255-type invalidity claims (e.g., actual-innocence or sentencing-error arguments) to qualify as “extraordinary and compelling reasons” would function as an end-run around § 2255’s carefully calibrated procedural safeguards and undermine finality and workability. Concepcion confirms broad discretion within authorized sentence-modification proceedings, but that discretion operates within the nature and limits of the proceeding and does not convert § 3582 into a collateral-review mechanism. Consistent with history and tradition of separating equitable leniency from legal invalidity, courts may consider post-sentencing factual developments and individualized circumstances under § 3582, but not relitigate the conviction/sentence validity reserved to § 2255.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a discretionary reduction of an otherwise lawful sentence for “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” but it does not confer authority to adjudicate the validity of the conviction or sentence—work Congress separately assigned to § 2255 with strict procedural limits on timeliness and successive petitions. Reading “extraordinary and compelling” to encompass § 2255-type claims would create an end-run around that detailed postconviction scheme, contrary to the Sentencing Reform Act’s baseline rule that a court “may not modify” a sentence except in narrow, enumerated circumstances. Dillon v. United States underscores that § 3582 proceedings are limited sentence-modification mechanisms, not plenary resentencings or vehicles for reconsidering the original sentence’s legality, and that structural limitation carries over to § 3582(c)(1)(A) even after the First Step Act expanded who may file the motion. Concepcion recognizes broad discretion within the authorized sentence-modification proceeding, but it does not license courts to use § 3582 to perform collateral review that Congress channeled into § 2255.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) authorizes a sentence reduction when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” exist and requires consideration of the § 3553(a) factors, and nothing in its text imposes the categorical exclusion the government seeks for circumstances that could also be framed under § 2255. Concepcion v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2389 (2022), reinforces that in sentence-modification proceedings Congress generally permits broad district-court discretion to consider intervening changes of law or fact absent an express limitation, and importing § 2255’s gatekeeping rules into § 3582 is an atextual constraint. Procedural fairness is preserved because § 3582 does not vacate a conviction or declare a sentence unlawful—district courts may treat such overlap as one factor in a totality inquiry while still denying relief under § 3553(a) or limiting re-litigation through ordinary doctrines (law of the case, waiver/forfeiture). A near-categorical bar would be pragmatically overinclusive, preventing courts from accounting for unjust sentencing consequences the First Step Act was designed to let judges evaluate directly once exhaustion is met.
